stories.title: Singapore Firms Dominate Southeast Asia Data Centre Funding, Account for 98% of US$11.5 Billion Raised: Report
stories.summary: Singapore-headquartered companies accounted for roughly 98 percent of the US$11.5 billion in data centre funding raised across Southeast Asia, according to a new report. The concentration underscores the city-state's role as the region's capital and deal-making hub even as physical builds spread to neighboring markets.
stories.why_it_matters: The figures confirm that while data center construction is migrating to Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand for land and power, the money and corporate control remain anchored in Singapore. For policymakers in neighboring states, it highlights the challenge of capturing more of the value chain; for investors, it reinforces Singapore-based platforms as the primary vehicles for regional exposure.

stories.title: Singapore Launches Liquid Cooling Standard for Data Centres in Tropical Climate
stories.summary: Singapore has launched a liquid cooling standard tailored for data centers operating in tropical climates. The standard provides technical guidance for deploying liquid cooling technologies needed to handle high-density AI workloads in hot and humid conditions.
stories.why_it_matters: As AI racks exceed what air cooling can handle, a tropical-specific standard gives operators and equipment vendors a common benchmark, reducing deployment risk in the region's climate. Singapore's move could become a reference point across Southeast Asia, accelerating liquid cooling adoption and influencing facility design requirements in neighboring markets.

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic

stories.content:
It accounts for the challenges presented by high temperatures and humidity, such as equipment corrosion

[SINGAPORE] Singapore has launched a new standard for data centres on adopting liquid cooling technologies in tropical areas, as demand for artificial intelligence workloads grows across South-east Asia.

The move follows the Republic’s latest award of 200 megawatts in new data centre capacity, and comes amid growing concerns about these facilities’ large energy and water consumption.

The new standard – dubbed the Singapore Standard (SS) 726 – builds on existing international standards for liquid cooling, while accounting for operational conditions in tropical climates.

It also recommends best practices on measuring and optimising water use, said the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) and Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG) in a Thursday (Aug 27) statement.

Both agencies developed SS 726 through the Singapore Standards Council, in consultation with industry players and experts.

## Design, deploy, integrate

Unlike traditional air cooling, liquid cooling uses fluids to transfer heat from hardware chips, reducing energy consumption at the data centre level by more than 30 per cent.

“However, tropical conditions such as high temperatures and humidity present additional challenges, including equipment corrosion, which can affect cooling efficiency and reliability,” IMDA and EnterpriseSG noted.

The standard addresses these issues with technical guidelines to design and deploy liquid cooling systems, manage potential risks, and integrate liquid cooling with existing air-cooled data centres.

IMDA deputy CEO Aileen Chia said that liquid cooling is “increasingly important to support the higher power densities required for AI and other advanced computing workloads”.

SEE ALSO

The authorities will continue to work with partners to “push the boundaries for data centre energy efficiency”, she added.

As part of a move towards green data centres, Singapore also previously launched the Tropical Data Centre standard and the Energy Efficiency of Data Centre IT Equipment standard.

stories.title: DCI's Sumit Mukhija: why certainty matters more than megawatts
stories.summary: The data centre industry is planning more capacity than ever, but DCI Data Centers CEO Sumit Mukhija says the increasingly scarce commodity is not megawatts; it is certainty that those megawatts can actually be delivered. Mukhija will explore that argument at the Sydney Cloud & Datacenter Convention on 17 September, where he will deliver the […]
stories.content:
The data centre industry is planning more capacity than ever, but DCI Data Centers CEO Sumit Mukhija says the increasingly scarce commodity is not megawatts; it is certainty that those megawatts can actually be delivered.

Mukhija will explore that argument at the **Sydney Cloud & Datacenter Convention on 17 September**, where he will deliver the keynote “The Capacity Paradox: Why Certainty, and not Megawatts, has become the Industry’s Scarcest Resource.”

The shift reflects the rapid change in the infrastructure market, Mukhija told W.Media ahead of next week’s event. Mukhija has spent more than three decades working across IT, cloud and data centre infrastructure, including more than a decade leading ST Telemedia Global Data Centres (STT GDC) in South Asia.

“A lot has changed in terms of scale, density and speed,” he says. “Over my career, we have gone from 3-5kW racks to 150-300kW today and potentially a MW per rack; and from data centres measured in tens of megawatts to campuses in the hundreds of megawatts, with some now approaching a gigawatt. Perhaps the biggest change, though, is the mainstreaming of AI.”

The resulting demands for compute, power, capital and more sophisticated cooling are changing the equation for customers, investors and operators. “For customers, time to market and increasingly time to compute are critical. For investors, much more capital needs to be committed upfront, often well before customer contracts are finalised, making the quality and bankability of those contracts important. For operators, the scale of the commitments and the associated delivery risk have increased significantly,” he explains.

That leaves all three groups asking essentially the same question. “The common theme is therefore ‘certainty’ [that is] how much can be delivered, when and where it can be delivered, and with what level of confidence,” he says.

“AI and technology cycles are getting shorter, while the underlying infrastructure supporting them can still take years to secure, approve and build. That is the paradox: we have more capacity planned than ever before, but certainty around when and how that capacity becomes real has become increasingly valuable,” he says.

### From announced MW to operational capacity

For Mukhija, the headline capacity attached to a project tells only part of the story. “I think it is important to recognise that projects simply carry different levels of certainty at different stages of their lifecycle,” he says.

Between planned capacity and an operational megawatt, he identifies a series of dependencies: land, capital, approvals, community acceptance, secured power and an energisation timeline, customer commitments, long-lead equipment, supply chains, design and execution. “So, beyond counting megawatts, we also need to understand the level of certainty behind those megawatts,” he says.

### Power is a question of timing

Power availability has consequently become less about a straightforward assessment of whether sufficient electricity exists and more about when it can actually reach the site. “Power is increasingly a time question as much as a capacity question,” Mukhija says. “Knowing that power will ultimately be available is very different from knowing when it can actually be energised.”

That affects DCI’s development strategy with its own facilities and the commitments it makes to customers. “We therefore focus not simply on how much power may ultimately be available, but on what is secured, when it can be energised, and when that capacity can actually be delivered to customers,” he says.

Mukhija says DCI distinguishes between secured capacity that can be delivered within a customer’s required timeframe and longer-term campus potential or future power availability. “We market secured power and capacity that can be delivered within the timelines our customers require, supported by land readiness, energisation timelines, the necessary approvals and investor confidence,” he explains.

For AI customers, he adds, that distinction can have direct economic consequences. “The timing of compute can have significant economic value. Our responsibility as an operator is to provide customers and investors with clarity on how much we can deliver, when we can deliver it, and the level of certainty behind that commitment,” he says.

### Uncertain technology cycles

The other side of the equation is the pace at which AI hardware and workloads are changing. A data centre may be expected to operate for decades, while the technology installed inside it can change within months.

Mukhija therefore argues against designing infrastructure too tightly around any particular generation of hardware. “The key is to build infrastructure that can remain relevant and be redeployed across multiple technology and investment cycles,” he says. “That means not locking the design too tightly to a particular chip, cooling architecture or today’s density. We need sufficient headroom for future densities and the flexibility to accommodate different compute and cooling architectures as they evolve.”

For Mukhija, that is another dimension of certainty. “Certainty is not knowing exactly what the future will look like. It is building infrastructure that remains valuable when the future changes,” he says.

**What makes a project credible?**

The same principle applies when customers, investors and governments assess the growing pipeline of Australian data centre projects. Mukhija’s test is whether the critical components of a project are coming together rather than simply how large the proposed campus is.

“It comes down to whether the key elements are actually coming together: land, secured power and timing, approvals and community acceptance, committed capital, customer demand, supply-chain readiness, adaptable infrastructure and an operator that can execute,” he says. “No single element is enough on its own.”

That assessment also feeds into a broader question about Australia’s attractiveness to infrastructure investors. “We have historically benefited from strong investor confidence, supported by stable institutions, transparent regulation and a predictable investment environment,” Mukhija says. “These are important advantages when competing for global infrastructure capital, and we should not take them for granted.”

He supports data centres taking responsibility for their impacts on infrastructure and communities, but says the cost of additional requirements needs to be considered alongside Australia’s competitiveness. “I fully support the principle that data centres should be responsible for their impact on infrastructure and communities. But some of the emerging requirements around operators funding upstream electricity and water infrastructure and supporting additional renewable generation will add significant costs to development,” he warns.

The issue, he argues, is whether those costs deliver corresponding benefits. “If these costs are incremental, without corresponding benefits in operating costs or greater certainty of delivery, we risk making Australia less cost-competitive relative to other markets in the region,” he says.

“We therefore need to get the balance right: responsible development and strong social licence, while preserving the investment certainty and competitiveness that have made Australia an attractive market in the first place,” he says.

Ultimately, Mukhija says the industry needs to change how it evaluates the capacity coming into the market. “Customers, investors and governments need to look beyond the headline megawatt figure and understand what sits behind it and the level of certainty around delivery,” he told W.Media. “Announced capacity is a number. Capacity with certainty is a promise you can underwrite.”

stories.title: The race to secure power without burdening the grid
stories.summary: AI is certainly changing the power mix, and the demand is huge. But how have bottlenecks changed the way data centers are planned and built?
stories.content:
With power demands for AI continuing to surge, data center operators are fighting to secure power quickly and reliably. The journey, however, doesn’t always now start with the grid.

Historically, developers selected a site based on fiber connectivity, line availability, incentives, and access to a strong workforce. Now, according to Cummins VP for power generation, Stiven Smith, grid connection delays have led to a wide industry rethink.

“The first question developers ask now is ‘how quickly can I secure power?’ When the grid tells them they need to wait five to seven years, they decide to take things under their own control,” he explains during a recent DCD>Talk. “The trend is: let’s secure power now and connect to the grid later.”

Cummins specializes in diesel and alternative fuel engines and generators. Smith is responsible for leading a team to solve prime power needs using natural gas and microgrids, integrating solar panels and battery energy storage systems (BESS).

What he’s witnessing now is other technologies emerging in recent years, as AI hyperscalers and colocation data centers started to consider natural gas prime power for their solutions. Within this, the development of on-site prime power solutions has become central to data center power strategies.

“Specifically for AI data centers, workloads are fluctuating and huge,” he says. “Power is needed now.”

The path to success for AI data centers depends on how quickly power can be secured, rather than depending on utilities, Smith adds. He advocates for alternative solutions, including behind-the-meter (BTM).

“The ‘bring-your-own-power’ model is paramount. You can decide when to turn it on, how to maintain it, and how to scale it,” he says. “In the US specifically, we are one of the four largest natural gas producers. Not only that, but we can extract it, compress it, and transport it. There is an extensive network across some states, so it’s a relatively cheap fuel source.”

He advocates for natural gas as the answer to 24/7 data center operations – and their ability to respond to current industry demands. In line with this, Cummins recently announced a new large-megawatt natural gas platform, which came after the company recognized a need from its customers and the wider market.

“Natural gas prime power technology isn’t new to us,” explains Smith. “The platform is moving to a 3.3MW generator … and is a continuation of our portfolio, based on understanding where the market will evolve in the future.”

Cummins’ platform is mainly designed to speed up time-to-power and accelerate deployment. The company is using an existing platform and scaling it with a longer cylinder block and additional cylinder heads, Smith explains.

“To address grid interconnection delays, the generator can be scaled from hundreds of megawatts to potentially gigawatts,” he adds. “You have that flexibility with the footprint.”

The platform also enables fast integration into microgrids and BTM requests, in addition to its ability to work in parallel with hybrid energy architectures.

“We currently have an extensive network of branches in every major city across the US,” Smith says. “That allows us to leverage proven natural gas technology with the ability to service and maintain it over the long term and provide an answer to the market.”

With consistent power the urgent need, Smith views data center power solutions migrating towards a more diversified energy portfolio – as the technology evolves to optimize chips.

“We’re learning every day,” he shares. “We understand we need to provide a base load of power and there are spikes in AI requests from chips. These are very large and still evolving, it’s almost impossible that one single technology will be able to meet every requirement.”

To secure power via natural gas, Cummins uses BESS to help regulate the load. Combining the two technologies with natural gas turbines means the turbines manage a portion of the base load, generators handle a second base load, and batteries manage the third and more fluctuating part.

Looking ahead, Smith foresees nuclear technologies one day entering the mix too.

“It’s a dynamic and evolving market. Natural gas is the primary answer now, but we expect more diversification in the future,” he says. “In my opinion, the winners will be companies that truly understand this complexity and can architect resilient solutions that are also economically attractive for developers.”

For operators looking to the future, he encourages them to secure power early, consider flexibility, to think about hybrid energy systems, and avoid losing sight of maintenance.

“Think beyond immediate power needs,” he adds. “There should be the ability to scale … and become more resilient. You’re no longer depending on just one source; you’re pulling several resources together into a single solution.”

stories.title: Kirin 9050 Pro proves Huawei's workaround. Malaysia is weighing the generation before it
stories.summary: Kirin 9050 Pro is the first commercial chip built on Huawei’s LogicFolding architecture. Malaysia is said to be considering Ascend 910C silicon that predates the architecture entirely. Huawei launched the Kirin 9050 Pro in Guangzhou on Monday, the first commercial chip to use the LogicFolding architecture the company has spent four months defending in research […] The post Kirin 9050 Pro proves Huawei’s workaround. Malaysia is weighing the generation before it appeared first on TechWire Asia .
stories.content:
- **Kirin 9050 Pro is the first commercial chip built on Huawei’s LogicFolding architecture.**
- **Malaysia is said to be considering Ascend 910C silicon that predates the architecture entirely.**

Huawei launched the Kirin 9050 Pro in Guangzhou on Monday, the first commercial chip to use the LogicFolding architecture the company has spent four months defending in research papers. *Bloomberg* reported the same day that Malaysia is seriously evaluating Huawei’s Ascend 910C accelerators for a RM2 billion (US$494 million) sovereign AI initiative.

The two developments are closer than they look, and the gap between them is the point. LogicFolding is the technology Huawei says will keep it competitive without access to extreme ultraviolet lithography. It has now been in a shipping product for one day. The Ascend 910C that Malaysia is reportedly considering predates it entirely.

The chip debuted in the Mate XT 2, a trifold handset starting at 19,999 yuan (US$2,980). Richard Yu Chengdong, chairman of Huawei’s consumer business group, said the Kirin 9050 Pro delivered a 42% overall performance improvement over the previous-generation Mate XTs and called it the most powerful Kirin the company has built. The device is also the first to run HarmonyOS 7, which began rolling out to existing Huawei phones on Monday.

https://x.com/Huawei/status/2096942699689726061

### What LogicFolding actually does

Chipmakers with access to the newest lithography tools improve performance mainly by printing smaller transistors. Huawei cannot, so it is buying performance with geometry instead.

Conventional 3D integration stacks largely self-contained dies on top of one another, like floors in a building that each operate independently. LogicFolding splits core computing functions across two active layers designed to work as a single unit.

Folding the circuit shortens the physical distance signals travel, cutting both delay and the energy lost in transit across the neural processing, graphics, central processing, and digital signal units that dominate a smartphone chip’s thermal budget.

That principle sits under what Huawei calls its Tau Scaling Law, introduced in a May paper by He Tingbo, chairwoman of the company’s Scientist Committee and president of its semiconductor business department. The paper claimed LogicFolding could reach transistor densities equivalent to a 1.4-nanometre process by 2031 without EUV machines, which remain blocked for sale to China under US-led export controls.

### The Kirin 9050 Pro numbers need reading carefully

Huawei published a third paper on ChinaXiv on Friday, and according to *South China Morning Post*, the tech giant addressed the objection analysts had raised most consistently, which is that stacking active logic vertically would trap heat. He wrote that measurements on the new chip turned the objection on its head. The paper said the chip ran cooler than its predecessor while packing 55% more transistors per square millimetre and cutting power consumption by up to 66% on some tasks.

Two caveats belong with those figures. The paper has not been peer-reviewed. And the density claim is measured against the Kirin 9030 Pro, while the 42% performance figure compares device generations, so the two headline numbers are not describing the same comparison. No independent teardown of the Kirin 9050 Pro has been published.

The approach also carries a manufacturing cost. Bonding two active silicon layers requires precise wafer thinning and microscopic vertical wiring, steps that can weigh on factory yields, according to Leslie Wu, chief executive of semiconductor consultancy RHCC, in a research note. Wu described LogicFolding as a compensatory route and a choice born of external constraints. For companies that can simply print smaller transistors on one layer, he said, the economics are less compelling.

### Malaysia’s decision sits on the other side of the roadmap

Venkat Somala, a researcher at Epoch AI, wrote on Friday that smartphone processors offered a far gentler starting point than AI chips. Smaller dies make production losses easier to absorb, lower power draw reduces the thermal problem, and high handset volumes give assembly lines the repetition they need to mature. Scaling the same architecture to Ascend accelerators, which are larger and run far hotter, would be considerably harder. Huawei has said it expects to rely on established 3D stacking for the rest of the decade before bringing LogicFolding to its flagship Ascend 990 around 2030.

That timeline is what regional buyers are actually purchasing against. Anyone evaluating Huawei AI silicon this year is evaluating pre-LogicFolding hardware, and *Bloomberg’s* reporting, quoting people familiar with the matter, suggests Malaysia is looking at the 910C rather than the newer Ascend 950 because the 950 remains in limited production. Supply, not architecture, is setting the terms.

The politics are unresolved as well. Malaysia’s deputy communications minister announced a national AI system running on 3,000 Ascend chips in May 2025, then retracted the statement within days. The investment ministry said at the time that Malaysia was committed to export control compliance while reaffirming its sovereign right to set policy in the national interest.

Washington has warned that use of the 910C could breach US export rules. *Bloomberg* reported that Anwar Ibrahim’s administration is also discussing a separate tender that would let Nvidia compete for the same contract.

Huawei is carrying the cost of the workaround on its own balance sheet in the meantime. First-half research and development spending rose 25% year on year to 121.4 billion yuan (US$18 billion) while net profit fell 36% to 23.8 billion yuan. Revenue grew 9.6% to 467.8 billion yuan, helped by a rebound in smartphone shipments and demand for its AI processors, and the company held 22.6% of the Chinese smartphone market in the second quarter, on a 19.4% jump in shipments, according to IDC.

stories.title: Singapore tables Digital Infrastructure Bill following industry feedback, pledges to streamline implementation
stories.summary: Singapore's government has tabled the Digital Infrastructure Bill after consulting industry, committing to a streamlined rollout that gives existing data centers a transition period to meet new energy-efficiency requirements. The legislation creates a formal regulatory framework for digital infrastructure resilience and sustainability.
stories.why_it_matters: The bill converts Singapore's data center policy from ad hoc moratoriums and pilot schemes into permanent law, giving operators regulatory certainty while hard-wiring efficiency standards into the market. Incumbent facilities gain breathing room through transition provisions, but new entrants and upgrades will face clearer compliance hurdles, shaping investment decisions across the region's most regulated hub.

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic

stories.content:
Existing data centre facilities will be given time to transition to energy-efficient requirements.

[SINGAPORE] The Singapore government tabled a bill to regulate data centres and cloud service providers, after respondents to an earlier public consultation sought greater clarity on its licensing regimes and implementation timeline.

The Digital Infrastructure Bill was presented for First Reading by Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information Tan Kiat How on Tuesday (Sep 8), following a three-week long public consultation between Jul 1 and Jul 22 on the proposed legislation.

The consultation, led by MDDI and the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), received feedback from 25 respondents, which included data centre operators, consultants and industry associations.

The feedback received mainly focused on how the licensing regimes would operate in practice, including transition arrangements.

As the legislation is implemented, MDDI and IMDA said they will aim to minimise the regulatory burden by streamlining licensing and reporting processes, while also recognising existing industry standards and certifications.

Some respondents also raised concerns that a proposed six-month period may not provide sufficient time for companies to determine if they need to be licensed and adhere to the regulatory requirements, as well as make any necessary arrangements.

The regulators clarified that the six-month period is for companies to apply for a licence, not to meet the new requirements.

Service providers and data centre operators that apply within the six-month window will be allowed to continue through the application process until their licence is granted, refused or withdrawn.

Existing data centre facilities will also be given time to transition to energy-efficient requirements, after respondents highlighted potential challenges in upgrading older facilities.

SEE ALSO

However, the regulators did not share how long existing data centres would be given to meet the requirements.

## Licensing regimes

First proposed in July, the Bill seeks to strengthen the security and resilience of major cloud services and data centres, as well as address the environmental sustainability of data centres in the Republic.

To address these needs, the Bill will establish two new licensing regimes that will apply to both existing and upcoming Singapore data centres.

The first regime seeks to manage operational risks and will apply to data centres with a critical IT load of at least 10 megawatts (MW) and major cloud service providers that generate at least S$100 million in average revenue in Singapore over the three preceding years.

The framework will establish a licensing regime which requires licensees to implement security and risk management measures, business continuity and disaster recovery plans.

Data centre operators under the first framework will be required to report specific incidents and disruptions to IMDA.

The second framework – which will apply to all data centres with a critical IT load of at least 3 MW – requires all licensees to meet facility-level energy-efficiency requirements, including power usage effectiveness requirements.

Under the second framework, licensed data centre operators will be required to track and record key sustainability metrics, as well as meet strategic and green energy requirements under the Data Centre Call for Action and Strategic Digital Infrastructure Scheme.

The regulators may consider including other efficiency requirements, such as water usage efficiency, in the future.

About two-thirds of Singapore’s approximately 70 data centres will fall within the licensing of the two frameworks.

Singapore currently has more than 1.6 gigawatts of data centre capacity as rising demand for computing power increases pressure on the Republic’s limited land, power and water resources.

The Bill will be debated at a future Parliament sitting, with the Second Reading tentatively scheduled for October.

stories.title: China Hits Japan With Anti-Dumping Measures for Semiconductor Chemical
stories.summary: This adds to the country’s retaliation in a diplomatic dispute over Taiwan
stories.content:
This adds to the country’s retaliation in a diplomatic dispute over Taiwan

CHINA unveiled preliminary anti-dumping measures on imports from Japan of a chemical used to make semiconductors, adding to its retaliation in a diplomatic dispute over Taiwan.

Companies importing Japanese dichlorosilane, used to process silicon wafers into semiconductors, are required to provide cash deposits of up to 99.2 per cent from Tuesday (Sep 8), Beijing’s Commerce Ministry said in a statement.

Beijing and Tokyo have been embroiled in a feud since November 2025, when Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi suggested Tokyo could deploy its military if China attempts to seize Taiwan, a self-ruled democracy claimed by Beijing.

Since then, China has responded with moves like warning travellers to avoid Japan and tightening some export controls.

The move comes ahead of Takaichi’s expected visit to the US in September. Chinese leader Xi Jinping also plans to meet US President Donald Trump in the White House on Sep 24.

Japan is the global leader in ultra-high purity dichlorosilane, though China has sought to expand upstream in the chip supply chain, nurturing research and development of key materials and tools.

The measures are part of a preliminary ruling resulting from an anti-dumping investigation China launched into dichlorosilane in January.

China’s Commerce Ministry said that dumping caused substantial harm to China’s domestic industry.

The deposit rates were set at 80.8 per cent for Denal Silane and 99.2 per cent for Shin-Etsu Chemical and other Japanese producers, the Commerce Ministry said.

SEE ALSO

Japan used to be China’s biggest supplier of dichlorosilane, until South Korea overtook it in 2025.

In July, imports from Japan were worth US$2.6 million, accounting for about 33 per cent of China’s total dichlorosilane imports, customs data show. BLOOMBERG

stories.title: Meta tests robots for data centre operations to manage costs
stories.summary: Meta is reportedly deploying robots from Watney Robotics, Kinova, and ABB inside its data centres to automate physical tasks such as server resets and cable connections. The initiative is aimed at improving operational efficiency and controlling rising labour costs as spending on AI infrastructure climbs, though it has raised job security concerns among data centre staff.
stories.why_it_matters: If successful, robotics could reshape data centre staffing models and operating cost structures across the hyperscale sector, pressuring rivals to follow suit. For the workforce, routine hands-on roles face automation risk, while demand may shift toward robot supervision and maintenance skills.
stories.content:
Meta is reportedly deploying robots from Watney Robotics, Kinova, and ABB in its data centres to automate physical tasks like server resets and cable connections. This move aims to enhance efficiency and manage rising labour costs as AI infrastructure spending increases. However, it also raises concerns among data centre workers about job security.

Highlights

Meta is deploying robots from Watney Robotics, Kinova, and ABB in its data centres.

Robots are being tested for tasks like server power cycling and network cable swapping.

The initiative aims to automate physical tasks and manage rising data centre labour costs.

Testing is underway at Meta's Altoona, Iowa, and New Albany, Ohio, data centres.

Facebook-parent Meta is reportedly testing robotics technology from vendors including Watney Robotics, Kinova, and ABB within its data centres to automate various physical tasks. This initiative comes as the company seeks to enhance operational efficiency and manage increasing labour costs amidst growing investments in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.The technology is being evaluated for tasks such as plugging in cables, resetting servers, and performing other physical maintenance. One experiment involves assessing whether a Kinova Gen3 robotic arm can handle power cycling servers, while another robot is being tested for swapping networking cables. Simpler devices are also in use for basic functions like pressing power buttons to restart equipment.

Operational impact and worker concerns

While Meta’s expansion into robotics could automate some physical tasks, potentially allowing it to operate its expanding data centre footprint with fewer personnel, it has raised concerns among current workers. One Meta data centre employee estimated that successful implementation could take over up to 80 per cent of some workloads.Meta spokesperson Francis Brennan stated that the company is investing significantly in training and hiring workers to build and operate its data centres, citing a shortage of skilled workers. Eric Xu, Meta’s senior manager for robotics, previously indicated that the long-term goal for robotics in data centres includes speeding up incident response, monitoring site conditions, and handling preventive maintenance.

Current limitations and testing grounds

Despite these advancements, the technology still faces limitations, including slow operating speeds, navigation challenges, battery downtime, and difficulty in reading equipment indicators. These constraints mean human intervention remains essential for many data centre operations.Meta is reportedly using its Altoona, Iowa, and New Albany, Ohio, data centres as testing grounds for these newer robotic deployments, including dual-armed machines for cabling tasks. Robotics experts suggest there is currently no proven solution capable of fully replacing human roles across the diverse range of data centre operations.

stories.content:
AI infrastructure provider Nscale has partnered with humanoid robotics company Figure for a multi-year AI compute deal, initially valued at US$3.5 billion and scalable to over US$6 billion. This collaboration could involve deploying 100,000 NVIDIA GPUs to support Figure's AI models and robots. The agreement highlights increasing demand for high-performance computing infrastructure in the rapidly evolving AI and robotics sectors.

Highlights

Nscale and Figure signed a multi-year AI compute partnership worth US$3.5 billion initially

The deal could lead to the deployment of 100,000 NVIDIA GPUs for Figure's AI models

Initial infrastructure deployment is planned for late 2027 in Barstow, Texas

Nscale will become Figure's preferred compute provider and take a stake in the robotics company

Nscale, a provider of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure and high-performance graphics processing unit (GPU) cloud services, has signed a multi-year partnership with Figure, a humanoid robotics company. This agreement involves an initial commitment of US$3.5 billion in computing resources, with plans to scale the deal to more than US$6 billion.The partnership is expected to support the deployment of 100,000 NVIDIA GPUs as Figure expands the computing infrastructure behind its AI models and robots. The planned infrastructure may utilise NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin platform, the company’s AI computing architecture. Initial deployment is scheduled for the second half of 2027 in Barstow, Texas.

AI Compute Infrastructure Focus

The collaboration will see Nscale become Figure's preferred compute provider and also involve Nscale taking a stake in Figure. The computing infrastructure is designed to support Figure’s Helix AI models, which power its humanoid robots.The companies intend to integrate computing, AI infrastructure, and software across the model development process, from training through deployment. They will also explore the potential use of humanoid robots within Nscale’s own supply chain.Josh Payne, Founder and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Nscale, highlighted the growth in inference and agentic AI, stating that Figure is pushing the boundaries of AI. Brett Adcock, Founder and CEO of Figure, noted that the expansion of humanoid robots is largely constrained by data and compute, with their AI model, Helix, becoming more capable with increased data and compute.Jensen Huang, Founder and CEO of NVIDIA, commented on the emergence of physical AI through humanoid robots, describing the partnership as activating the robotics flywheel by training Figure’s models on NVIDIA Vera Rubin via Nscale’s AI cloud, validating them in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, and deploying them on NVIDIA GPUs in Figure’s robots.

stories.title: DigitalBridge opens Tokyo office to expand in Japan
stories.summary: DigitalBridge has opened a Tokyo office, giving the digital infrastructure investor closer access to deal flow as Japanese demand for data centres and network connectivity grows on the back of AI and cloud adoption. The move marks a deeper commitment to one of Asia's fastest-expanding digital infrastructure markets.
stories.why_it_matters: A permanent Tokyo presence lets DigitalBridge compete more effectively for Japanese assets against global and domestic rivals, potentially accelerating investment into the market. For Japan, it adds another well-capitalised buyer at a time when power, land, and connectivity constraints make experienced operators valuable.
stories.content:
![DigitalBridge opens Tokyo office to expand in Japan](https://datacenternews.asia/uploads/story/2026/09/08/neutral-tokyo-office-cityscape-data-center-network-cables-digital-illustration-story-318464.webp) 

# DigitalBridge opens Tokyo office to expand in Japan

Tue, 8th Sep 2026 (Today)
![Karen Joy Bacudo](<https://datacenternews.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyMSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--019183c634a09650fab653c6e35bf96cd3b99fba/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/images%20(22)%201.webp>) 

DigitalBridge has opened an office in Tokyo to lead the investment firm's expansion in Japan.

Soichiro Suda, who joined the company as Managing Director earlier this year, will lead investment activities in Japan and serve as its senior representative in the market. His remit includes identifying, evaluating, executing and managing investments across DigitalBridge's digital infrastructure portfolio.

The move gives DigitalBridge a local base in a market where it already invests in data centres, telecoms towers and connectivity assets. The new office is intended to help source deals, support closer work with portfolio companies and deepen ties with local partners.

Japan has become a growing focus for international infrastructure investors as demand for computing capacity and network links rises across the economy. That demand has been tied to artificial intelligence, broader cloud adoption and businesses' digital transformation.

Earlier this year, DigitalBridge launched Nippon Gateway Infrastructure, an enterprise data centre platform formed with JEXI. The platform was built around a portfolio of data centre facilities acquired from NEC.

Its holdings in Japan also include JTOWER, an independent telecommunications infrastructure company, and Vantage Data Centres, which operates hyperscale data centre capacity in Osaka. Together, those assets give the firm exposure across several segments of the digital infrastructure market as it expands its presence in the country.

### Japan focus

The broader market backdrop has also drawn investor attention. The Japanese government has announced a long-term economic strategy calling for ¥101.6 trillion in combined public and private investment in artificial intelligence and semiconductors through 2040, equivalent to about USD $630 billion.

That policy direction has reinforced expectations of heavier spending on the digital systems needed to support data processing, storage and communications. Data centres and telecoms infrastructure are among the assets expected to benefit if those investment plans translate into projects on the ground.

DigitalBridge, based in Boca Raton, manages digital infrastructure investments across sectors including cell towers, data centres, fibre, small cells and edge infrastructure. It has operated in the broader digital investment market for more than three decades and has offices across North America, Europe, the Middle East and Asia.

Suda brings more than 30 years of experience across energy, infrastructure advisory, asset management and investment banking. Before joining DigitalBridge, he was Chief Investment Officer at Japan Extensive Infrastructure.

He also spent seven years as a Managing Director at Macquarie Asset Management, where he worked on infrastructure investments in Japan. Earlier roles included Director positions at Ernst & Young Transaction Advisory, where he led infrastructure advisory, and at Storm Harbour Japan.

Before that, Suda spent 17 years at Mitsubishi Corporation in a range of energy and natural gas roles. His work there included project development in Australia, business development in Malaysia, treasury and finance, and liquefied petroleum gas marketing across Asia.

DigitalBridge's senior leadership said the Tokyo opening reflects Japan's importance to its strategy in Asia and the strength of its existing portfolio in the country. The firm has been active in the market for several years, but the new office marks a shift toward a more permanent local operating presence.

Marc Ganzi, Chief Executive Officer of DigitalBridge, linked the opening to the firm's existing footprint in towers and data centres.

"Japan has been an important market for DigitalBridge for many years, and we have built a differentiated platform spanning towers, hyperscale, and enterprise data centers," said Ganzi. "Soichiro's leadership, together with the opening of our Tokyo office, strengthens our ability to support the growth of our portfolio and continue investing behind Japan's growing demand for AI, cloud, and connectivity infrastructure."

Justin Chang, Senior Managing Director and Head of Asia at DigitalBridge, said Suda's background would support the firm's local activity.

"Japan is one of the most attractive digital infrastructure markets in Asia, with world-class enterprises and growing demand for AI, cloud, and connectivity infrastructure," said Chang. "Soichiro's deep experience across infrastructure investing, advisory, and finance strengthens our local investment capabilities and relationships in Japan. He plays an important role in advancing our investment activities and supporting our portfolio companies and partners across the market."

Soichiro Suda, Managing Director at DigitalBridge said the company sees a broad set of opportunities in the country.

"Japan is a highly strategic market for DigitalBridge, with significant opportunities emerging across data centers, connectivity, and the broader digital infrastructure ecosystem," said Suda. "Over the past several months, I've seen firsthand the strength of DigitalBridge's platform, global capabilities, and relationships in the Japanese market. I look forward to building on that foundation alongside our investment teams, portfolio companies, and local partners."

stories.title: AI data centres make grid access key to power deals
stories.summary: Grid congestion is emerging as a central factor in data centre transactions, adding risk and a scarcity premium to deals as AI-driven electricity demand rises sharply. Securing grid access and power capacity is increasingly determining valuations and deal structures in the sector.
stories.why_it_matters: Power availability is overtaking location and capital as the binding constraint on data centre growth, meaning sites with secured grid connections command premium pricing. Investors and developers must now underwrite energy risk as rigorously as real estate fundamentals, and markets with constrained grids may see development slow.
stories.content:
![AI data centres make grid access key to power deals](https://datacenternews.asia/uploads/story/2026/09/08/james-cameron-steven-jack-and-matt-eastwick-story-318462.webp) 

![Sean Mitchell](https://datacenternews.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyOSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--a929a91c2a04d9af95ed98b14ed4d405bc70c1a7/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/IMG_3092.webp) 

Artificial intelligence demand and data centre expansion are reshaping global power markets, with grid access becoming a central factor in project viability, according to JLL.

Its analysis points to a sharp rise in electricity demand after years of relative stability or decline, with data centre growth emerging as a major driver across the United States, Europe and Asia Pacific. In Asia Pacific, data centre capacity is projected to rise from 32GW to 57GW by 2030, while global capacity could reach 200GW over the same period.

This shift is colliding with grid systems built for large, centralised power stations rather than a faster-growing, more dispersed mix of renewable generation and large-scale computing facilities. In several markets, queues to connect new projects now stretch to four years or longer, and some regions have paused new connections altogether.

That pressure is increasing the importance of transmission access in energy, property and digital infrastructure deals. Investors are placing greater weight on whether an asset already has a connection or a credible path to securing one, turning power access from an operational issue into a valuation question.

Hyperscale technology companies are also increasing spending as they build out cloud and AI infrastructure. JLL said hyperscalers had announced USD $200 billion of infrastructure spending for 2026, up 51% from 2025.

The trends are not uniform across regions. In the United States, interconnection reform and exposure to merchant power markets are altering deal structures. In Europe, regulatory change is moving at different speeds between countries. In Asia Pacific, the pace of data centre construction is outstripping grid planning in several markets.

Steven Jack, Head of Energy and Infrastructure Advisory, EMEA, at JLL, described the scale of the shift in power demand.

"We've seen a generational shift in power demand as a result of data centres and AI," Jack said. "This was not on the radar until very recently. Utilities that were forecasting modest growth are now grappling with figures nearly double their previous estimates. For any energy developer, without a grid connection, you don't have a project. For investors, this grid congestion translates directly into risk, but it also creates a scarcity premium for assets that provide or secure grid access. In a world of geopolitical uncertainty, generating your own power is about energy sovereignty or energy autonomy, and it's simply the cheapest way to produce power today."

### Storage focus

Battery energy storage systems are becoming more prominent as developers and investors look for ways to manage intermittency, reduce stress on constrained grids and improve the economics of renewable supply. Their growth reflects a broader effort to build more flexibility into power systems as data centre demand rises.

Matt Eastwick, Group Head and Senior Managing Director, Energy and Infrastructure Advisory, U.S., at JLL, said batteries had become a key part of that response.

"Batteries are a very important component and asset in that balancing act," Eastwick said. "They act as shock absorbers for constrained grids, charging when power is cheap and abundant, then discharging when demand and price are high. We're in a brave new world. Power demand is rising faster than grids were built to handle. Capital is available, but certainty is harder to find. In this environment, winners will be those who factor grid constraints and power availability into their investment decisions from day one."

JLL also highlighted its recent advisory role on the disposal of a 395MW/790MWh operational battery storage portfolio in the UK, which it described as the largest operational sale of its kind in Europe. The firm said the transaction set a new pricing benchmark for the market.

### Regional models

Grid bottlenecks are also changing the relationship between energy producers and major electricity users. Large technology groups are taking a more direct role in securing generation, including through purchases of operating renewable assets, to reduce reliance on uncertain connection timelines and wholesale market volatility.

One recent example cited by JLL involved a Bitcoin miner in Texas buying an operating wind farm that the firm had been marketing to secure its own power supply. The case illustrates the premium some users are prepared to pay for dependable access to electricity.

In Asia Pacific, investors are increasingly treating grid status and location as the first point of due diligence for development assets, particularly in liberalised electricity markets. JLL identified Australia, India, Japan and the Philippines as examples where connection status can have the biggest effect on valuation.

James Cameron, Head of Energy and Infrastructure, APAC, at JLL, said the pressure was producing new deal structures in the region.

"In liberalised markets in Asia Pacific, such as Australia, India, Japan and the Philippines, status and location of grid connection is the first question for investors and has the largest valuation impact for development assets," Cameron said. "In Australia, where legislation is expected to require data centre developers to ensure new renewable power generation matches additional capacity, we're seeing a range of innovative models, from joint ventures to the inclusion of batteries in data centre design to facilitate grid connection. While the solution will differ depending on circumstances, it is clear we will see many more partnership opportunities and innovative solutions between data centre and energy clients across the region."

stories.title: Data centre boom could push Australian warehouse rents sharply higher
stories.summary: JLL warns that Australia's surging data centre pipeline could push economic rents for conventional warehouses in Sydney and Melbourne more than 100 percent above current market levels, as operators compete with logistics users for industrial land. The firm estimates the national data centre investment pipeline now runs into the tens of billions of Australian dollars.
stories.why_it_matters: Logistics tenants and industrial landlords face sharply higher occupancy costs as data centres outbid them for suitable land near power and fibre. This could reshape urban industrial markets, push warehouses further from city centres, and raise costs across supply chains serving Australia's two largest cities.
stories.content:
Australia’s expanding data centre pipeline could put significant upward pressure on industrial property costs in Sydney and Melbourne, with competition for land potentially pushing economic rents for conventional warehouses more than 100 percent above current market levels, according to commercial real estate firm JLL.

The firm estimates Australia’s data centre investment pipeline now exceeds AUD 155 billion, making the country the world’s third-largest destination for data centre investment. The capacity pipeline has grown from 451MW in 2015 to 1.2GW today, while a further 16.2GW is under construction or planned, according to its figures.

New South Wales and Victoria account for 91.3 percent of that future capacity, concentrating the impact on metropolitan industrial markets where available land is already constrained. JLL’s modelling indicates that competition from data centre developers could have a substantial impact on the economics of conventional industrial development.

For a standard 20,000 square metre warehouse, economic rents in Sydney’s Outer Central West could rise to 88 percent above current prime rents under a high-growth scenario, while Melbourne’s West could see rents reach 132 percent above current market rates.

The figures represent JLL’s modelling of the economics required to develop new industrial space, rather than forecasts that warehouse tenants will necessarily see their rents increase by those percentages.

### Not just land

The impact is already extending beyond land transactions. JLL said major suppliers of data centre components had collectively leased more than 100,000 square metres of warehouse space across Sydney over the past year, while data centre operators were also establishing logistics hubs close to their facilities. Construction-sector occupiers accounted for 177,800 square metres of gross industrial take-up over the past year, or 4.2 percent of total demand – almost twice the 10-year average share.

Rick Warner, JLL Australia director of research and report author, said the modelling showed the structural pressure emerging in the industrial market. “Our feasibility modelling shows economic rents are already 30% to 43% above current market rents in Sydney, and 64% to 103% above in other Australian markets, even before factoring in land premiums paid by data centre developers that will ultimately elevate land values further,” Warner said.

JLL’s Matthew Lee, executive director and co-head of Australian data centres, added: “For investors, I am not concerned at all about having too many data centres in the pipeline, because demand is – and will continue to be – strong,” Lee said. “The greater concern is around the time it will take projects to come to market.”

Lee also pointed to a change in the potential customer base for new facilities, with developers increasingly talking to a broader range of hyperscale and “neocloud” customers rather than a small group of traditional hyperscalers.

The concentration of development in Sydney and Melbourne could eventually encourage a shift towards regional markets, JLL said. Locations with greater land availability and access to renewable energy resources could become increasingly attractive as developers look beyond the established metropolitan markets.

JLL also expects the number of developers operating at scale in Australia to roughly double over the next five years as overseas groups, predominantly from Asia and the US, enter the market.

stories.title: Energy diversification in Singapore has to make business sense: Gan Siow Huang
stories.summary: The Republic has a vital role in bringing together capabilities that manage complex energy flows
stories.content:
The Republic has a vital role in bringing together capabilities that manage complex energy flows

[SINGAPORE] Singapore companies’ efforts to diversify energy supplies have to be based on market and commercial sense, said Minister of State for Trade and Industry Gan Siow Huang.

The question companies have to ask “is not simply can we diversify; it is ‘where is additional resilience worth paying for?’”, Gan said in a speech to oil and gas industry players on Tuesday (Sep 8).

She was speaking at the S&P Asia Pacific Petroleum Conference, held at the Raffles City Convention Centre.

Some 60 per cent of South-east Asia’s crude imports have traditionally come from the Middle East.

But the US-Iran war posed a major disruption. Before the conflict, 20 million barrels of oil moved through the Strait of Hormuz, but between March and May, that fell to just 2.7 million barrels per day.

Gan noted that the region’s heavy reliance on Middle Eastern crude is based on commercial value: Gulf producers operate at scale and are close to Asian markets. Many regional refineries are configured to process medium and heavy Gulf crudes.

As such, diversification does not mean abandoning established relationships but creating more options.

Gan said: “The objective here is not to maximise the number of crude grades a refinery can process. It is to maintain a practical portfolio of alternatives that have been tested, understood and also that can be activated quickly when normal supply is disrupted.”

She acknowledged that flexibility carries a cost, as alternative crude “may involve longer shipping distances, different yields, additional storage or blending, and changes to refinery operations”.

SEE ALSO

Each company will therefore have to make commercial decisions based on its own assets, markets and risk exposure.

## Preparing for the next shock

Gan also highlighted that energy resilience requires building capabilities across the value chain, such that alternative sources can actually be delivered when needed.

“That means having the right producer, but also the vessel, insurance, storage, financing, liquidity, infrastructure and risk-management capabilities to execute the transaction, particularly when markets are volatile,” she said.

Singapore has a vital role in bringing together capabilities that manage these complex energy flows.

For instance, oil giants ADNOC and Petrobras have tapped Singapore as a regional base, while India’s Bharat Petroleum established its first international trading office here to expand crude procurement and refined-products trading.

Gan noted that the next energy shock may come from geopolitics, extreme weather, infrastructure failures, cyber attacks or a sudden shift in demand.

While governments will need to provide stable policy and investment frameworks, companies “must decide where resilience is worth the cost and build that flexibility into their operations”, she said.

“And the wider energy ecosystem – traders, financiers, shipowners, logistics providers and technology companies – must continue to find better ways to connect supply and demand to manage risk.”

The French AI startup plans to treble its Singapore headcount as it expands in South-east Asia

[SINGAPORE] French artificial intelligence startup Mistral has raised three billion euros (US$3.5 billion) in a Series D funding round, valuing the three-year-old company at more than 21 billion euros.

The Series D, announced on Tuesday (Sep 8), is the largest equity fundraising round completed by a European technology company, said Mistral.

Samsung Electronics led the round, with the Scaleup Europe Fund, managed by EQT, and existing investor PSG Equity as co-leads.

New investors include funds and accounts managed by BlackRock and Luxembourg. Existing backers such as ASML and Nvidia also participated.

The funds will be used to expand Mistral’s frontier AI research, as well as scale compute capacity for training AI models. Infrastructure expansion and commercial and geographical growth will also be fuelled by the capital injection.

Mistral currently operates in 20 countries, including Singapore, where it opened an office in January 2025. The startup plans to treble its headcount in Singapore as it chases growth in South-east Asia.

Globally, Mistral supports more than 125 enterprises in their AI transformation.

“This round means we can move faster on R&D, products, infrastructure and keep giving organisations the ability to run AI at scale, on their own terms,” said Arthur Mensch, co-founder and CEO of Mistral.

Samsung Electronics’ investment comes after a Series C round led by Dutch semiconductor player ASML.

stories.title: A tenth of Malaysia's electricity consumption is from data centres, says energy regulator
stories.summary: Malaysia's Energy Commission says data centres now account for nearly a tenth of the country's total electricity consumption. The regulator expects power demand from the sector to climb further by the end of the year.
stories.why_it_matters: The figure quantifies the strain the data centre boom is placing on Malaysia's grid and will sharpen debate over tariffs, renewable energy obligations and approval conditions for new facilities. Utilities, policymakers and developers now face pressure to align capacity expansion with grid investment, or risk backlash from consumers facing rising costs.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
PETALING JAYA (Sept 8): Data centres make up nearly a tenth of Malaysia’s electricity consumption, according to the Energy Commission, with demand for power expected to pick up further by the end of the year.

Electricity consumption by data centres has risen to 9.28% of total consumption, said EC chief executive officer Siti Safinah Salleh, adding that the warmer weather also saw cooling systems using more power.

More data centres expected to come online in November would also push up consumption, she noted.

Malaysia has attracted RM95.8 billion in data centre and cloud-computing projects in the first half of this year alone, the Malaysian Investment Development Authority said recently.

Most of Malaysia's data centre invesetments are concentrated in Johor. The Knight Frank Data Centre Atlas 2026 report released in July said data centres in the state had a live capacity of 1,110 megawatts (MW) and an incoming pipeline capacity at 8,542MW. Data centre capacity is often measured by the a amount of power it can draw on.

By comparison, the EC's MyEnergyStats portal records Malaysia's installed electricity generation capacity at 27,333MW as of 2025, with a peak demand of 21,049MW recorded on May 28 last year. 

    

Deputy Minister Datuk Seri Fadillah Yusof previously told Parliament in July that data centres are expected to consume around one third of Malaysia’s electricity supply by 2035. At the time, data centres accounted for 7% of electricity consumption.

The government has hinted at putting the brakes on data centre investments, with the Investment, Trade and Industry (MITI) saying projects will be approved only after ensuring that energy and water supply capacity is sufficient.

SEOUL (Sept 8): South Korea's demand for power in the coming years is set to surge on plans by chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix to expand production and the building of new AI data centres, according to the country's energy minister.

Those AI-driven power needs alone will lift South Korea's demand for power by 25 to 30 gigawatts, the Minister of Climate, Energy and Environment Kim Sung-whan said in a *Reuters* interview this month.

On top of that, the country will also need to contend with increased power demand due to the shift to electric vehicles from gasoline-engine cars and to heating via electricity rather than gas, he added.

His comments come ahead of a government plan to unveil next month an update to the nation's long-term energy roadmap, extending it by two years to 2040. One key focus is whether South Korea will announce plans to build more nuclear reactors.

Kim declined to comment on how many more reactors he thinks the country needs, saying the matter was being reviewed by experts. But he described nuclear energy as "an essential element to consider within the power generation structure of our energy mix."

If an extra 25 to 30 gigawatts were to come from nuclear energy alone, that would be equivalent to the capacity of about 20 reactors based on the current standards of a South Korean-designed unit.

Asia's fourth-largest economy currently has 26 nuclear reactors and nuclear energy accounts for just under a third of the country's power needs.

Samsung and SK Hynix — two of the world's biggest chipmakers whose products are essential to AI infrastructure — have pledged to build new factories in the country's southwest as part of an 800 trillion won (US$590 billion) "mega project" announced by the government this year.

"Projects originally planned to be built by around 2045 have been significantly accelerated and are now due to be completed by the early 2030s," Kim said.

Kim also said that several US tech companies including Nvidia NVDA.O have expressed interest in building data centres in South Korea because of its dependable power supply.

While South Korea aims to boost renewables — which account for 11% of its power needs currently — reliance on nuclear energy is unavoidable for now despite its safety risks, he said.

A poll by the state-run Korea Energy Information Culture Agency found 79% of 2,000 respondents supported including new nuclear plants in the roadmap.

But in May, a civic group in Ulsan, a potential site for new plants, collected more than 10,000 signatures opposing additional reactors on safety grounds.

Kim said he did not expect the planned cluster of chip plants in the country's southwest to require a new nuclear plant, because six reactors already operate there alongside existing solar and wind farms.

Instead, regions such as Seoul, which depend on electricity transmitted from that area, would need additional solar plants or even liquefied natural gas plants, he said.

Other energy sources in South Korea include coal, which accounts for 29% of its power needs currently, while gas accounts for 27%.

The country has 60 coal-fired power plants and aims to phase them out by 2040. That said, 20 of them will still have a legal design lifespan beyond that point in time and one option could be to keep them as emergency backup power.

"It's a kind of safety power reserve. You never know what might happen, so completely dismantling everything could put us in a difficult situation," Kim said.

stories.title: Malaysia Already Studying Potential Role of Nuclear Energy, Says Chang
stories.summary: GEORGE TOWN (Sept 8): Malaysia is already studying the potential role of nuclear energy in its future energy mix, with the government also undertaking preparatory work in technology, talent and regulatory development.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
GEORGE TOWN (Sept 8): Malaysia is already studying the potential role of nuclear energy in its future energy mix, with the government also undertaking preparatory work in technology, talent and regulatory development.

Minister of Science, Technology and Innovation Datuk Chang Lih Kang said, however, the ongoing preparations did not mean the government had decided to adopt nuclear energy as a source of power.

"Of course, we are now doing the preparatory work. It does not mean that we have already made a decision but we need to be prepared so that our regulatory framework is ready, our talent is ready, and at the same time, we need to ensure the industry is also ready.

"Three areas fall under the Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation's (Mosti) portfolio in relation to the nuclear energy preparedness efforts (technology, talent and regulatory development), while the other areas will be considered by the Ministry of Energy Transition and Water Transformation (Petra)," he said.

He told reporters this after officiating the ninth edition of the Engineering, Science and Technology Congress (ESTCON 2026), organised by Universiti Teknologi PETRONAS (UTP), here on Tuesday. The event was also attended by UTP Chancellor Tan Sri Dr Mohd Hassan Marican.

Chang said that Malaysia's growing energy demand, driven by the expansion of strategic sectors such as semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing and hyperscale data centres, required the country to consider a full range of options for its longer-term energy needs.

He said the preparations required more than technological assessments, stressing that Malaysia also needs strong scientific and engineering capabilities, a robust regulatory and safety framework, a highly competent workforce and domestic industry readiness.

"Malaysia must ensure that its economic and technological growth are supported by energy that is secure, affordable and increasingly sustainable, as well as that Malaysia must also strengthen its capabilities in strategic and emerging technologies, including AI, advanced materials, space and nuclear technologies," he said.

Chang noted that the efforts were aligned with the National Science, Technology and Innovation Policy 2030, which provides strategic direction for strengthening Malaysia's science, technology and innovation (STI) capabilities through research and development, future-ready talent, technology adoption and innovation.

The minister also said Malaysia's STI ambitions also extended to the regional level, with greater Asean cooperation needed in areas such as energy connectivity, digital infrastructure, research and emerging technologies.

He added that such collaboration would be crucial in strengthening the region's collective resilience and competitiveness amid rapid technological change, climate challenges and geopolitical tensions.

stories.title: Thailand Maps Plan to Source 89% of Power from Clean Energy
stories.summary: Thailand is considering generating 89% of its electricity from cleaner sources by 2050 as it formally puts a more ambitious long-term power plan to public consultation.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
(Sept 8): Thailand is considering generating 89% of its electricity from cleaner sources by 2050 as it formally puts a more ambitious long-term power plan to public consultation.

The draft released Tuesday sets a minimum clean-power share of 65%, with several more aggressive options also under consideration. The most renewable-heavy scenario would lift that share to 89%, well above the target outlined by Energy Minister Akanat Promphan last month.

The plan comes as the country faces rising electricity demand from data centres and advanced manufacturing while trying to cut its reliance on imported natural gas, which still supplies most of its power. That dependence leaves Thailand exposed to swings in global fuel prices, a risk highlighted by the Middle East conflict and higher gas import costs.

“Achieving net zero is a key challenge as global trade and investment increasingly focus on cutting greenhouse gas emissions,” Prasert Sinsukprasert, the Energy Ministry’s permanent secretary, said Tuesday. “Major global companies, particularly data centre operators, are choosing Thailand as an investment hub because they have confidence in the country’s power policies and its commitment to clean energy.”

*Bloomberg News* first reported last month that the government was preparing to sharply increase its use of renewable energy and add nuclear power to the national plan. Renewables currently account for about 15% of the power mix.

The country has attracted billions of dollars of investment in data centres, cloud computing and advanced manufacturing, adding to pressure on the government to ensure there is enough electricity without pushing up household power bills.

Under the draft, about 51,000MW of new power capacity would be added through 2037, with most of it coming from solar, wind and battery storage, alongside new gas and nuclear power.

The most renewable-heavy option could require about 700 billion baht (RM85.99 billion) of investment through 2050 in power networks, batteries and other equipment needed to support a much larger share of renewable energy.

The plan also includes up to 9,000MW of nuclear capacity. The government is studying small modular reactors and micro modular reactors as options for future nuclear power plants.

Thailand last revised its 25-year power development plan in 2023, before the latest energy shock and the surge in electricity demand linked to artificial intelligence. The country still aims to reach net zero by 2050.

stories.summary: Selangor's state government is closely tracking water and power supply capacity as data center development accelerates, Menteri Besar Amirudin Shari said. The monitoring effort reflects concerns that the state's infrastructure may struggle to keep pace with the concentration of new facilities.
stories.why_it_matters: Selangor hosts much of Malaysia's data center growth, and any utility constraints there directly affect project timelines for the industry's biggest operators. The state government's posture suggests future approvals may be conditioned on resource availability, pushing developers to secure dedicated power and water arrangements earlier in the planning cycle.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
SEPANG (Sept 8): The Selangor government is closely monitoring water and power supply capacity amid the rapid expansion of data centres in the state, said Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Amirudin Shari.

He said the state would not approve data centre projects without ensuring adequate water and electricity supply, amid growing public concerns over the industry’s resource requirements.

“We are very aware of the concerns of the public related to power and water supply, and we are monitoring closely.

“Without enough water, definitely the data centre cannot be approved in Selangor,” he told reporters after witnessing the handover of vacant possession for NCT Smart Industrial Park (NSIP) Phase 1 here on Tuesday.

Amirudin was commenting on NCT Alliance Bhd’s (KL:NCT) recent announcement that it had signed a term sheet for the proposed sale of a 100-acre land parcel within NSIP for a data centre development that could support up to 800 megawatts (MW) of capacity.

Amirudin said every data centre application must obtain approval from the Federal Data Centre Task Force, with power supply requirements to be cleared by Tenaga Nasional Bhd (KL:TENAGA) and water supply by Pengurusan Air Selangor Sdn Bhd.

He said the state government is confident that its water supply capacity would be sufficient, particularly with the Rasau Water Supply Scheme expected to provide an additional 350 million litres per day (MLD), while the capacity could reach 700 MLD upon full completion of its first phase.

He also stressed that the state government is encouraging data centre operators to adopt water-recycling systems and technologies that could reduce water consumption for cooling purposes.

“We are encouraging the recycling of water … so that the processed water is not discharged, but instead recycled within each data centre,” he said.

Amirudin said the rapid expansion of data centres could also generate wider economic benefits by supporting the development of the electrical and electronics (E&E), chip and semiconductor sectors.

He added that Selangor had also introduced a 30% policy to ensure small and medium enterprises (SMEs) benefitted from data centre operations in the state.

stories.title: Malaysia Expects Nine GW of Gas-Fired Power Capacity by 2032 to Meet Rising Demand
stories.summary: PETALING JAYA (Sept 8): Malaysia expects about nine gigawatts (GW) of gas-fired power capacity to be deployed by 2032 as the country manages growing electricity demand, while progressively phasing out coal-fired generation.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
PETALING JAYA (Sept 8): Malaysia expects about nine gigawatts (GW) of gas-fired power capacity to be deployed by 2032 as the country manages growing electricity demand, while progressively phasing out coal-fired generation.

Minister of Economy Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir said the capacity would form part of the country’s efforts to manage electricity demand, with the last coal-fired power plant expected to be retired in 2044.

Akmal Nasrullah said energy demand was showing an upward trend, driven by factors including population growth and higher consumption from energy-intensive sectors such as data centres.

“In terms of the projection for energy demand, definitely we see a pattern of increase. One is population growth.

“But number two, there is also an increase in energy consumption by high-usage sectors such as data centres,” he told reporters after the Energy Regulatory Insights 2026 here on Tuesday.

He said weather and climate conditions could also change energy demand patterns, particularly as hotter conditions increase the need for cooling systems and air conditioning.

Against this backdrop, Akmal Nasrullah said managing energy demand would become as crucial as managing energy supply over the next five to 10 years.

“I think for the next five to 10 years, Malaysia must really remain disciplined enough to ensure our system is continuously upgraded, not just in terms of the power produced, but also the grid and infrastructure, so that our system remains affordable, safe and sustainable,” he added.

He said energy planning should not only focus on the megawatts that need to be deployed in the system, but also on energy efficiency and conservation.

Akmal Nasrullah said the planning would need to be managed by the Ministry of Energy Transition and Water Transformation and the Energy Commission to ensure the country could manage demand, while remaining committed to sustainability efforts and reducing the energy sector’s carbon footprint.

Earlier in his keynote address, Akmal Nasrullah outlined three priorities for the next phase of energy reform, starting with the need for a competitive and progressive energy market with clear and predictable rules and transparent access arrangements.

Secondly, he said expanding generation capacity must be supported by a modern grid that is intelligent, visible, secure and flexible, with grid modernisation under the 13th Malaysia Plan regarded as essential economic infrastructure to enable investments to connect faster, improve system efficiency and support reliable economic growth.

Thirdly, Akmal Nasrullah said energy efficiency must be treated as an energy resource in its own right, as it could reduce operating costs, ease pressure on the system and strengthen competitiveness.

He said the first National Energy Efficiency Action Plan (NEEAP) exceeded its original target, delivering cumulative electricity savings of 60,886 gigawatt-hours, equivalent to RM16.1 billion in savings, from 2016 to 2025.

Under NEEAP 2.0, Malaysia is targeting an 11.6% reduction in energy demand against the business-as-usual scenario by 2035, which is expected to help lower energy costs, ease pressure on the system and support more productive and competitive economic activity.
